Corneal cholesterol/phospholipid deposition reduces stromal transparency.

nodes.description: Progressive loss of corneal transparency produces bilateral, slowly progressive visual impairment at the level of the whole organism; advanced disease often requires keratoplasty. Glare and photophobia may accompany the more superficial forms.

In macular corneal dystrophy, loss-of-function mutations in CHST6 abolish corneal N-acetylglucosamine-6-O-sulfotransferase activity. Keratan sulfate, a major corneal glycosaminoglycan whose sulfation confers water solubility, is left poorly sulfated or unsulfated; the resulting less-soluble proteoglycan accumulates within keratocytes and the stromal matrix, disrupting fibril organization and corneal hydration and producing progressive opacification.

evidence.reference_title: Macular corneal dystrophy type I and type II are caused by distinct mutations in a new sulphotransferase gene.
evidence.snippet: we identify a new carbohydrate sulphotransferase gene (CHST6), encoding an enzyme designated corneal N-acetylglucosamine-6-sulphotransferase (C-GlcNAc6ST), within the critical region of MCD type I

nodes.description: Bilateral corneal opacification from abnormal stromal deposits is the defining clinical finding across the stromal dystrophies.

evidence.snippet: small opacities are seen throughout the stroma of the entire cornea and give the cornea a cloudy appearance

nodes.description: In congenital stromal corneal dystrophy, heterozygous truncating DCN mutations yield a dominant-negative decorin. Decorin normally regulates the diameter and uniform spacing of stromal collagen fibrils; the abnormal protein accumulates and disorganizes the collagen lattice, so the cornea is diffusely cloudy from birth with flake-like stromal opacities.

evidence.reference_title: Congenital stromal dystrophy of the cornea caused by a mutation in the decorin gene.
evidence.snippet: revealed a frameshift mutation in the DCN gene (c.967delT) that encodes for decorin

evidence.reference_title: Congenital stromal dystrophy of the cornea caused by a mutation in the decorin gene.
evidence.snippet: truncated decorin binds to collagen in a suboptimal way, disturbing the regularity of corneal collagen fibril formation and thereby causing corneal opacities
Congenital stromal corneal dystrophy is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner

nodes.description: The unifying lesion of the group is inherited, non-inflammatory deposition of abnormal material within the corneal stroma. The deposited substance differs by form: abnormally sulfated keratan sulfate (macular, CHST6), cholesterol and phospholipid (Schnyder, UBIAD1), disorganized collagen fibrils from defective decorin (congenital stromal, DCN), or mutant TGFBI protein (granular and lattice). In each case the accumulating material progressively disrupts the ordered stromal collagen lattice that is required for corneal transparency.

nodes.description: Regardless of the deposited substance, accumulation within the corneal stroma scatters incident light and progressively reduces corneal transparency. This tissue-scale loss of stromal clarity is the shared final common lesion of the group.

nodes.description: Progressive bilateral reduction in visual acuity results from loss of corneal transparency; advanced disease often requires keratoplasty.

In the granular and lattice (TGFBI-associated) dystrophies, missense mutations in TGFBI produce a misfolded transforming growth factor beta-induced protein (TGFBIp / keratoepithelin) that accumulates as insoluble deposits in the stroma. Deposit morphology is mutation-specific (hyaline in granular type 1, amyloid in lattice, mixed in granular type 2 / Avellino). This arm is curated in depth in the subtype-level entry TGFBI_Corneal_Dystrophies.yaml; it is represented here for completeness of the stromal-dystrophy group.

nodes.description: In Schnyder corneal dystrophy, mutant UBIAD1 remains bound to HMG-CoA reductase and blocks its sterol-accelerated ER-associated degradation, so reductase accumulates and local cholesterol synthesis is dysregulated. The excess cholesterol and phospholipid are deposited in the corneal stroma (often as crystals), reducing transparency; many patients also have systemic hypercholesterolemia.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in the UBIAD1 gene on chromosome short arm 1, region 36, cause Schnyder crystalline corneal dystrophy.
evidence.snippet: A mutation in UBIAD1 was identified in all six families
